title: How overlap is measured, with a worked example
objectives: Calculate overlap by adding the smaller weight of each shared stock.
body_md:
The common method adds up, for every stock both funds hold, the smaller of its two weights. Worked example (illustrative, top holdings only): Bank 1: 9% in Fund A, 8% in Fund B, counted 8%. IT company 1: 7% and 6%, counted 6%. Bank 2: 6% and 7%, counted 6%. Energy company: 5% and 4%, counted 4%. Consumer company: 4% and 0%, counted 0%. Overlap from these stocks: 24%. Across the full portfolios, other shared stocks would add to this figure. Overlap tools on fund-research websites do this calculation from the latest published portfolios.

| Stock | Weight in Fund A | Weight in Fund B | Counted (smaller) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bank 1 | 9% | 8% | 8% |
| IT company 1 | 7% | 6% | 6% |
| Bank 2 | 6% | 7% | 6% |
| Energy company | 5% | 4% | 4% |
| Consumer company | 4% | 0% | 0% |
| Overlap from these stocks |  |  | 24% |

> **Investor takeaway:** Note the portfolio date when using an overlap tool: portfolios change as managers trade.
example: Shared stocks counted at 8% + 6% + 6% + 4% = 24% overlap from four top holdings alone.
say: Add the smaller weight of each shared stock.
A stock held by only one fund counts 0%.
never: Count shared stocks only, ignoring weights.
